Writing a model in R

Source: vignettes/ast.Rmd
ast.Rmd
library(multimod)

multimod models are usually read from a source file: read_gams() and read_gmpl() turn a GAMS or MathProg model into the structure described here. This vignette builds the same kind of object directly in R, which is the way to write a new model, to generate one programmatically, or to understand what the readers produce. The model is a small capacity-expansion problem: three technologies supply electricity to two regions at least cost. It ships with the package as example_models$toy; the code below is the file that built it.

The parts of a model

A model is a list of named components, each a small S3 object:

Component Constructor Holds
sets new_set() the index values of a dimension
mappings new_mapping() tuples over several sets, used as domains
parameters new_parameter() data indexed by dimensions
variables new_variable() decision variables, with a domain and bounds
equations new_equation() left side, relation, right side, over a domain

The sides of an equation are expressions: trees of AST nodes built with ast_variable(), ast_parameter(), ast_expression(), ast_sum() and their relatives. Every renderer (as_gams(), as_latex(), the LP matrix) is a walk over that tree.

Sets

A set names a dimension and lists its values.

techs   <- c("coal", "gas", "wind")
regions <- c("north", "south")

sets <- list(
  tech   = new_set("tech",   desc = "generation technologies", data = techs),
  region = new_set("region", desc = "model regions",           data = regions)
)
sets$tech
#> <AST set> tech

Mappings

A mapping is a table of tuples over one or more sets. Mappings serve as domains: an indexed variable or equation exists for exactly the tuples of its domain mapping, which is how sparse models stay sparse. Here every technology may be built in every region, so the domain is the full grid.

tuples <- expand.grid(tech = techs, region = regions, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

mappings <- list(
  mTR = new_mapping("mTR", desc = "technology x region pairs",
                    dims = c("tech", "region"), data = tuples),
  mR  = new_mapping("mR",  desc = "regions",
                    dims = "region", data = data.frame(region = regions))
)
mappings$mTR$data
#>   tech region
#> 1 coal  north
#> 2  gas  north
#> 3 wind  north
#> 4 coal  south
#> 5  gas  south
#> 6 wind  south

Parameters

A parameter declares its dimensions and carries a data frame with one column per dimension plus value.

parameters <- list(
  pCapCost = new_parameter("pCapCost", desc = "annualised capacity cost, EUR/kW",
    dims = "tech",
    data = data.frame(tech = techs, value = c(120, 70, 90))),
  pVarCost = new_parameter("pVarCost", desc = "variable cost, EUR/MWh",
    dims = "tech",
    data = data.frame(tech = techs, value = c(30, 55, 0))),
  pAvail = new_parameter("pAvail", desc = "availability factor",
    dims = c("tech", "region"),
    data = transform(tuples, value = c(0.85, 0.85, 0.90, 0.90, 0.35, 0.25))),
  pDemand = new_parameter("pDemand", desc = "annual demand, MWh",
    dims = "region",
    data = data.frame(region = regions, value = c(1000, 600)))
)
parameters$pAvail
#> <AST parameter> pAvail
#>   dims:  [tech,region]

Variables

Variables declare dimensions, a domain mapping, a type and bounds. A scalar variable has dims = character(0).

variables <- list(
  vCap = new_variable("vCap", desc = "installed capacity, kW",
                      dims = c("tech", "region"), domain = "mTR",
                      vtype = "positive", bounds = list(lo = 0)),
  vGen = new_variable("vGen", desc = "generation, MWh",
                      dims = c("tech", "region"), domain = "mTR",
                      vtype = "positive", bounds = list(lo = 0)),
  vCost = new_variable("vCost", desc = "total system cost, EUR",
                       dims = character(0))
)

Expressions

Inside an equation, symbols are referenced rather than declared: ast_variable() and ast_parameter() take the name and the index symbols, given as ast_dims(). ast_expression() combines two nodes with an operator, and ast_sum() sums an expression over index symbols.

gen   <- ast_variable("vGen", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region"))
avail <- ast_parameter("pAvail", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region"))
cap   <- ast_variable("vCap", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region"))

limit <- ast_expression("*", avail, cap)
node_type(limit)
#> [1] "expression"
limit
#> <AST expression> *
#>   lhs :
#> <AST parameter> pAvail
#>   dims:  [tech,region] 
#>   rhs:
#> <AST variable> vCap
#>   dims:  [tech,region]

Rendering is a method on the node, so an expression can be checked before it is used:

as_gams(limit)
#> [1] "pAvail[tech,region] * vCap[tech,region]"
as_latex(limit)
#> [1] "\\mathsf{pAvail}_{\\texttt{tech},\\texttt{region}}  \\cdot  \\bm{\\mathit{vCap}}_{\\texttt{tech},\\texttt{region}}"

Equations

An equation has a left side, a relation ("==", "<=", ">="), a right side and a domain. The domain mapping decides for which tuples the equation is generated.

eqCapLim <- new_equation("eqCapLim", desc = "generation is limited by capacity",
  dims = c("tech", "region"),
  lhs = gen, rhs = limit, relation = "<=",
  domain = ast_mapping("mTR", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region")))

eqDemand <- new_equation("eqDemand", desc = "demand is met in every region",
  dims = "region",
  lhs = ast_sum(ast_dims("tech"), ast_variable("vGen", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region"))),
  rhs = ast_parameter("pDemand", dims = ast_dims("region")),
  relation = ">=",
  domain = ast_mapping("mR", dims = ast_dims("region")))

eqCost <- new_equation("eqCost", desc = "total cost",
  dims = character(0),
  lhs = ast_variable("vCost", dims = ast_dims()),
  rhs = ast_sum(ast_dims("tech", "region"),
    ast_expression("+",
      ast_expression("*", ast_parameter("pCapCost", dims = ast_dims("tech")),
                          ast_variable("vCap", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region"))),
      ast_expression("*", ast_parameter("pVarCost", dims = ast_dims("tech")),
                          ast_variable("vGen", dims = ast_dims("tech", "region"))))),
  relation = "==")

eqDemand
#> <AST equation> eqDemand
#>   domain:  mR[region] 
#>   relation:  >= 
#>   lhs:  sum([tech]vGen[tech,region]) 
#>   rhs:  pDemand[region]
as_latex(eqCost)
#> [1] "\\begin{flushleft}\n\\subsection*{\\textbf{eqCost} -- \\textit{total cost}} \n\\quad$\\textbf{eqCost}$\n\\begin{equation*}\n\\begin{adjustbox}{max width=\\textwidth}\n$\\begin{aligned}\n&\\bm{\\mathit{vCost}}_{} = \\sum_{\\texttt{tech}, \\texttt{region}} \\mathsf{pCapCost}_{\\texttt{tech}}  \\cdot  \\bm{\\mathit{vCap}}_{\\texttt{tech},\\texttt{region}}  +  \\mathsf{pVarCost}_{\\texttt{tech}}  \\cdot  \\bm{\\mathit{vGen}}_{\\texttt{tech},\\texttt{region}} \\\\\n\\end{aligned}$\n\\end{adjustbox}\n\\end{equation*}\n\\vspace{1em}\n\\end{flushleft}"

The model

new_model() assembles the components. The objective is declared as the equation that defines it, the variable it defines and the sense.

toy <- new_model(
  name = "toy", desc = "two-region capacity expansion",
  sets = sets, mappings = mappings, parameters = parameters,
  variables = variables,
  equations = list(eqCapLim = eqCapLim, eqDemand = eqDemand, eqCost = eqCost),
  objectives = list(list(equation = "eqCost", variable = "vCost",
                         sense = "minimize"))
)
toy
#> Model: toy
#> Description: two-region capacity expansion
#> Sets:  2 
#> Mappings:  2 
#> Aliases:  0 
#> Parameters:  4 
#> Variables:  3 
#> Equations:  3

Every constructor validates its node against the AST schema as it is built (ast_schema() lists the node types and their fields), so a malformed node is refused where it is written. validate() checks the assembled model: every symbol referenced in an equation must be declared, with matching dimensions.

v <- validate(toy)
v$valid
#> [1] TRUE

The text backends write indexed expressions with short iterator names (sum{t in tech} in MathProg, for t in tech in Julia). A model built in R has none until add_index_aliases() derives them from the set names:

toy <- add_index_aliases(toy)
unlist(toy$index_aliases)
#>   tech region 
#>    "h"    "r"

Solving

The matrix route needs no external software: model_to_lp() builds the constraint matrix from the equations and the data, and solve_highs() passes it to the HiGHS solver (the ‘highs’ package).

lp <- model_to_lp(toy)
dim(lp$A)
#> [1]  9 13
r <- solve_highs(toy, attach = FALSE)
r$objective
#> [1] 198000
head(r$primal[r$primal$value > 0, ], 10)
#>        j symbol     i1     i2    lo    up      vtype       value reduced_cost
#>    <int> <char> <char> <char> <num> <num>     <char>       <num>        <num>
#> 1:     3   vCap   wind  north     0   Inf   positive   1111.1111            0
#> 2:     4   vCap   coal  south     0   Inf   positive    666.6667            0
#> 3:     9   vGen   wind  north     0   Inf   positive   1000.0000            0
#> 4:    10   vGen   coal  south     0   Inf   positive    600.0000            0
#> 5:    13  vCost   <NA>   <NA>  -Inf   Inf continuous 198000.0000            0

The file routes render the same model for an external solver: write_gmpl() for GLPK, write_jump() for Julia and write_pyomo() for Python; vignette("multimod") lists them with their solve_*() counterparts.

mod_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".mod")
write_gmpl(toy, file = mod_file)
cat(head(readLines(mod_file), 12), sep = "\n")
#> # Model: toy
#> # two-region capacity expansion
#> 
#> set tech;  # generation technologies
#> set region;  # model regions
#> 
#> 
#> set _IF_;  # Singleton set for GAMS $ operator emulation
#> 
#> set mTR dimen 2;  # technology x region pairs
#> set mR dimen 1;  # regions

Saving and exchanging the model

model_to_json() serialises the whole model, including the AST, in the language-neutral JSON format defined by ast_json_schema(); model_from_json() reads it back. This is the interchange format for other implementations of the model structure.

json <- model_to_json(toy)
back <- model_from_json(json)
identical(names(back$equations), names(toy$equations))
#> [1] TRUE
as_gams(back$equations$eqDemand)
#> [1] "eqDemand[region]$mR[region]..\n  sum(tech, vGen[tech,region]) =g=\n  pDemand[region];"

save_model() and load_model() write a model as a workspace directory with its data tables in CSV or Arrow files; see the “Model workspace” article on the package website.
